title: Defending against vendor lock-in
subtitle: The cost of leaving is decided when you choose, not when you want to leave
whyItMatters: Every external service is easy to enter and hard to exit, and the gap between those two is exactly how much bargaining power they hold over you at the next renewal.
openingQuestion: When is the cheapest moment to prepare for leaving a vendor?
openingOptions: When the contract is nearing its end and the two sides begin renegotiating the terms of it
When they raise the price or the quality of the service starts to visibly deteriorate
Once the team has used it long enough to know exactly which features it actually needs
explanation: The cost of leaving is not a fixed number - it grows with every week of further integration, and it grows fastest early on while the decisions about data shape are still being made. The other three moments are all points where that cost has already peaked, and they are also the moments when the other side holds the most bargaining power.

diagram.label: Build a thin separating layer immediately
Keep data in a portable shape
Cost of leaving stays a known quantity

realWorldExample.description: A team integrated a notification service in three weeks, calling the vendor's library directly from fourteen places in the code. Two years later the vendor quadrupled the price. The team estimated eighteen months to move, mostly not because of the fourteen call sites but because notification history, message templates and user subscription state all lived inside the vendor's system in a shape no other vendor could read.

sections.text: Being locked in is not an event, it is a quantity that grows. This lesson is about keeping it at a known level, and why every measure has to be taken before it is needed.
Three kinds of lock-in, by how hard they are to undo

items: Call-site lock-in: your code calls their library directly. Annoying, but effort undoes it
Data lock-in: your data sits in a shape only they understand. This is the expensive kind
Process lock-in: how the team works has bent around the tool. Nobody counts this one at all

sections.text: Most exit plans estimate only the first kind, because it is the only one you can count by searching the code. Then the move runs five times over, because of the other two, and neither of them shows up in any search.
Four measures, ordered by value per hour spent

items: A thin separating layer between your code and their library, written on day one
A periodic copy of the data in a common format, even while nobody needs to read it
A second vendor running for real on a small share of traffic, not merely a proof of concept
One page saying what you would do if you had to leave, refreshed at every renewal

sections.label: A thin layer, not a thick abstraction
sections.text: The common mistake on hearing this advice is to build an abstraction trying to cover every feature of every possible vendor. That costs ten times as much and is always wrong, because you are designing for a party you cannot yet name. The right layer wraps only what you actually use, thin enough to read in five minutes, and its value is gathering every point of contact into one place rather than hiding the differences.
A second vendor running for real is nothing like a proof of concept

A proof of concept demonstrates that integration is possible. One percent of real traffic through a second vendor demonstrates a great deal more: that your data genuinely moves, that the team genuinely operates both, and that your migration estimate rests on work done rather than work imagined. It is also the only item on this list the other side can see.

left.label: Prepared in advance
left.text: Costs a few days at the start and keeps the cost of leaving a known quantity. Bargaining power intact at renewal.

right.label: Prepared when needed
right.text: Costs nothing at first. By the time it is needed, leaving costs more than any price rise the other side could invent.

lines: The cost of leaving is decided when you choose, not when you want to leave.
The expensive kind of lock-in is in the data, and no search of the code will find it.

quiz.question: Which kind of lock-in costs most when leaving a vendor?
options: Call-site lock-in, because the number of places in the code is usually far larger than expected
Data lock-in
Contractual lock-in, because the penalties for terminating early are typically very heavy
Process lock-in, because the team has to relearn its whole way of working with a new tool
quiz.explanation: Call sites can be undone with effort and counted by searching the code. Data sitting in their shape has to be converted, and that conversion is usually larger than the entire original integration put together.

quiz.question: Why should the separating layer be thin rather than cover every feature?
options: Because new joiners find an abstraction with many invented concepts of its own hard to follow
Because a thick layer slows performance by routing every call through additional function layers
Because you are designing for a party you cannot yet name
Because a thick layer needs updating every time the vendor releases some new capability
quiz.explanation: An abstraction is only correct when you know what it must cover. Designing for every possible vendor is designing for none, so it costs ten times as much and still has to be rewritten on the day you genuinely move.

quiz.question: Why is one percent of real traffic worth more than a proof of concept?
options: It creates a standby option ready
It allows an objective comparison of actual service quality between the two vendors involved
It keeps the team in practice with the second vendor so switching later feels less unfamiliar
It proves the data moves and the team can operate both
quiz.explanation: All three of the others are real benefits. The first is the one a proof of concept cannot give: it turns your migration estimate from a guess into a measurement taken on work already done.

quiz.question: An exit plan estimates three months and the move takes eighteen. What is the usual cause?
options: The plan could only count the lock-in that lives in the code
The old vendor was uncooperative about exporting the data out of their system cleanly
The team was pulled onto other work, so the migration never got the priority it needed
The new vendor lacked some features, so those had to be built during the migration itself
quiz.explanation: The other three all happen and all are incidents. The first is the rule: a code search returns a specific and credible-looking number, and it is precisely that credibility that stops anyone going to look for the other two kinds.

quiz.question: When should the one-page exit plan be refreshed?
options: Every time the team adds another integration point with the current vendor's platform
At every contract renewal
Quarterly, alongside the regular review of the other technical risks in the system
Whenever there are signs the vendor is about to change its pricing or its terms
quiz.explanation: Renewal is the one moment on this list where the cost-of-leaving figure actually gets used. Refreshing it just before sitting down at the table is how a document becomes an advantage.

keyTakeaways: The cost of leaving grows with every week of integration, fastest at the start
Data lock-in is the expensive kind and no code search finds it
A thin layer wraps what you use, not every vendor you might one day pick
One percent of real traffic is worth more than any proof of concept

practicePrompt.question: Integration took 3 weeks across 14 call sites. The exit estimate allows 3 weeks for the code. What is the largest missing piece?
options: Converting historical data into a shape the new vendor can read
The time to negotiate the contract and complete the legal formalities with the new vendor
The effort of rewriting documentation and retraining the team on the new tooling
The period of running both vendors in parallel to compare results before switching off the old
practicePrompt.explanation: The other three all have to be added and all are measured in weeks. Data conversion is measured in months, because it depends on whether the new vendor has an equivalent concept at all - and where it does not, you have to build one.

summary.keyIdea: Keep the cost of leaving a known quantity by doing the work before you need it
summary.commonMistake: Estimating a migration by counting call sites in the code
summary.action: Find data your team holds that exists only in one vendor's shape.

application.title: Four things, on day one
application.message: A thin separating layer. A periodic data copy in a common format. One percent of traffic through a second vendor. One page describing the way out.
application.secondary: All four are cheap in the first week and nearly impossible after the second year.
